Diseases of Infancy & Childhood

Pathology · LE 3 · Trans 01 · Romil M. Aguirre, MD

What this lecture covers

Children are not merely little adults. Their diseases are not merely variants of other diseases. Many childhood conditions are unique, or at least take distinctive forms in this stage of life.

The lecture moves from causes of death by age group (USA vs Philippines) to the major disease groups of infancy and childhood:

Stages of development & causes of death→ Congenital anomalies→ Prematurity & FGR→ Hazards: NRDS, NEC→ Perinatal infections→ Fetal hydrops→ Inborn errors of metabolism→ SIDS→ Tumors & tumor-like lesions

Learning objectives

  • Identify the causes of death in the different age groups in infancy and childhood.
  • Recognize more common diseases during infancy and childhood.
  • Identify the etiology, pathogenesis, morphological changes, and manifestations of the recognized diseases.

❗ Must Know: red-exclamation points in this lecture
  • Congenital anomalies: most common cause of mortality in the 1st year (USA)
  • Prematurity: 2nd most common cause of neonatal mortality (behind congenital anomalies) in the USA
  • Intrauterine infections: major cause of preterm labor
  • Fetal abnormalities → proportionate FGR: symmetric growth restriction
  • Placental abnormalities → disproportionate FGR: asymmetric growth retardation
  • NRDS: most common cause of RDS in newborn
  • Sacrococcygeal teratoma: most common teratoma in childhood
  • Childhood malignant tumors: tendency to regress or differentiate spontaneously
  • Leukemia (ALL): #1 peak, most deaths in <15 y/o than all others combined
  • Disseminated neuroblastoma in neonates: "blueberry muffin baby"
  • Neuroblastoma prognostic variables noted by doc: Age, Schwannian stroma, MYCN
  • Wilms tumor: most common primary renal tumor in children

I–II. Introduction, Stages of Development & Causes of Death

Why study these? p. 1

  • Children are not merely little adults. Their diseases are not merely variants of other diseases.
  • Many childhood conditions are unique, or take distinctive forms in this stage of life.
    • These should be properly studied, especially their pathology, so they can be properly managed.

A. Infant Mortality Rate p. 1

19702014
USA (general population)205.8 ↓
Philippines59.312.6 (2010)

Rates per 1,000 live births. Worldwide range: Afghanistan 110.6 vs Slovenia 1.8 (2014).

  • The declining rates can be attributed to:
    • Better prenatal care, especially in developed countries
    • More effective methods of monitoring the condition of the fetus
    • Judicious resort to cesarean section before term when there is evidence of fetal distress
    • Availability of the NICU has significantly lowered neonatal and infant mortality rates

Key points p. 2

  • Philippines: the top causes of death among all the age groups are mostly infectious in nature.
    • Due to challenges in managing / controlling infectious diseases as a developing country.
    • Congenital anomalies are now third in 1-4 years old in the PH.
  • USA: congenital anomalies are the top in <1 year and second in 1-4 years.
    • There are less infectious causes of death in the USA. We can only see it at 5-9 years old, which is caused by pneumonia.
  • Accidents (unintentional injuries) are the top cause of death in the USA for 1-4, 5-9, and 10-14 years.

III. Congenital Anomalies

Definition p. 2

  • Anatomic defects that are present at birth.
    • Some may be clinically apparent in later years (e.g., cardiac defects and renal anomalies).
  • Congenital means "born with".
  • Does not imply or exclude genetic basis.
    • For example, in congenital syphilis, this is more of an infectious process rather than genetic or hereditary.
❗ Must Know
Most common cause of mortality in the 1st year (USA)

A. Errors in Morphogenesis

Congenital anomalies related with errors in organ and tissue development:

MalformationDeformationDisruptionSequenceMalformation Syndrome

Malformation Must Know p. 2-3

Definition: Intrinsically abnormal developmental process

Cause: single gene or chromosome defect (genetic in nature), but commonly multifactorial (e.g., gene defect + environmental cause)

Extent: may involve a single body system (e.g., congenital heart defects, anencephaly or absence of brain) or may involve many organs

ExampleLecture notes
PolydactylyPresence of multiple digits
Little functional consequences when they occur in isolation
SyndactylyFusion of digits
Little functional consequences when they occur in isolation
Cleft Lip / Cleft PalateLittle functional consequence when they occur in isolation
Compatible with life
Malformation SyndromeCleft lip and cleft palate associated with Trisomy 13
Neonate died of severe cardiac defects
Congenital Heart DefectsTruncus arteriosus
Ventricular septal defect
Lethal malformationMidline structures are fused or ill-formed

Deformation Must Know p. 3

Definition: Extrinsic disturbance of development

Pathogenesis: localized or generalized compression of the growing fetus by abnormal biochemical forces, leading to structural abnormalities

Most common underlying factor: UTERINE CONSTRAINT

  • Between the 35th and 38th weeks of gestation, there is rapid increase in the size of the fetus that outpaces the growth of the uterus.
    • The relative amount of amniotic fluid also decreases.
  • Amniotic fluid normally acts as a cushion between the fetus and the maternal womb.
    • Even the normal fetus is subjected to some form of uterine constraint.
  • When this uterine constraint is exaggerated → the fetus has problems growing → structural abnormalities.

Clubbed feet

  • An example of congenital deformation
  • Feet are turned inwards due to compression of the growing fetus in the maternal womb affecting the lower limbs
  • Often component of Potter (or oligohydramnios) sequence

Factors that increase the likelihood of excessive compression

Maternal factors (limit space in the womb)Fetal or Placental factors
  • 1st pregnancy
  • Small uterus
  • Malformed (bicornuate) uterus
  • Leiomyomas
  • Oligohydramnios (decrease amount of amniotic fluid)
  • Multiple fetuses
  • Abnormal fetal presentation

Disruption Must Know p. 4

  • Results from secondary destruction of an organ or body region that was previously normal in development.
  • Unlike congenital malformation, disruption involves an extrinsic disturbance in organ development.
  • NOT hereditary and therefore does not pose a risk for subsequent pregnancies.

Amniotic band (classic example)

  • The amnion suddenly ruptures, forming an amniotic band.
    • The band may attach, encircle, or compress parts of the developing fetus.
  • Effect depends on what the band encircles:
    • Limb → distal atrophy or may amputate the leg / structure
    • Face or head → craniofacial defects
    • Abdomen → visceral defects

Sequence Must Know p. 4

  • Congenital anomalies occur singly in half of the cases. In the other half, multiple anomalies are noted.
  • In Sequence, there is a cascade of anomalies triggered by one initiating aberration.
  • The multiple anomalies may be explained by a single localized aberration in organogenesis (malformation, disruption, or deformation) that sets into motion secondary effects in other organs.
  • Example: Potter sequence

Potter Sequence (Oligohydramnios) Must Know p. 4

There is decreased amniotic fluid or oligohydramnios which may cause some form of uterine constraint that will restrict the growing fetus and might cause deformations.

Causes of decreased amniotic fluid (maternal, placental, or fetal abnormality)

  • Chronic leakage of amniotic fluid due to rupture of amnion
  • Uteroplacental insufficiency (resulting from maternal hypertension or severe toxemia)
  • Renal agenesis: kidneys have not developed properly
    • Fetal urine is a major component of amniotic fluid.

Pathogenesis (Figure 10)

Renal agenesisAmniotic leakOthers
↓
OLIGOHYDRAMNIOS (→ also results in amnion nodosum)
↓
FETAL COMPRESSION
↓
Pulmonary hypoplasiaAltered faciesPositioning defects of feet (clubbed feet) & handsBreech presentation

Classic structural defects (Figure 9)

  • Flattened facies
  • Positional abnormalities of the hands and feet (clubbed feet)
  • Hips may be dislocated
  • Due to compression of the chest wall, the lungs may be hypoplastic
  • Amnion nodosum (nodules in the amnion)
Exam Trap (Review Q8)
Infant with flattened facies, clubbed feet, and dislocated hips → Potter sequence.
Explained by rupture of fetal membranes, renal agenesis, or uteroplacental insufficiency due to maternal hypertension.
Maternal diabetes mellitus is the EXCEPT.

Malformation Syndrome Must Know p. 4

  • Involves multiple congenital anomalies and cannot be explained on a single, localized initiating defect.
    • 📣 Lecturer In contrast to sequence, where the congenital anomalies can be attributed to one initiating cause.
  • The constellation of multiple congenital defects is believed to be pathologically related.
  • Often caused by a single etiologic agent (like viral infection or specific chromosomal abnormalities) which simultaneously affects several tissues.

Errors in morphogenesis at a glance

TypeNatureKey featureExample
MalformationIntrinsicIntrinsically abnormal developmental processPolydactyly, syndactyly, cleft lip/palate, CHD
DeformationExtrinsicCompression of growing fetus. Most common factor: uterine constraintClubbed feet
DisruptionExtrinsicSecondary destruction of a previously normal organ. Not hereditaryAmniotic band
SequenceCascadeMultiple anomalies from one initiating aberrationPotter sequence
Malformation SyndromeMultiple, relatedCannot be explained by a single localized initiating defect. Single etiologic agentCleft lip/palate + cardiac defects (Trisomy 13)

Review answer key: Malformation → intrinsically abnormal. Disruption, Deformation → extrinsic disturbance. Sequence → extrinsic.

B. Definition of Important Terms

Table 6. Organ Specific Terms Must Know p. 4-5

TermDefinition
AgenesisComplete absence of an organ or its associate primordium
AplasiaAbsence of an organ due to failure of growth of the existing primordium
AtresiaAbsence of an opening (ex. Esophageal atresia: no opening in the esophagus)
Hypoplasia / HyperplasiaDecrease / increase number of cells
Hypotrophy / HypertrophyDecrease / increase size of cells
DysplasiaAbnormal organization of cells, usually is a precursor of carcinoma or malignancy
Do Not Confuse
Agenesis = no primordium at all.
Aplasia = primordium exists but fails to grow.
Atresia = absence of an opening.

C. Causes of Congenital Anomalies

How often is the cause known? Must Know p. 5

Although we are learning a great deal about the molecular basis of some congenital anomalies, the exact cause remains unknown in 40-60% of cases.

40-60%Unknown
20-25%Multifactorial (genetic & environmental)
12-25%Genetic
10-13%Environmental

Table 7. Causes of Congenital Anomalies p. 5

CauseFreq (%)Examples / Notes
Genetic Causes
Chromosomal Aberrations10-15Chromosomal syndromes such as Down syndrome, trisomies, Turner syndrome, Klinefelter
Mendelian Inheritance2-10Single gene mutations like holoprosencephaly: the most common developmental defect of the forebrain and mid face in humans
Environmental Causes
Maternal / Placental infections2-3Toxoplasmosis, syphilis, CMV, HIV
Rubella embryopathy: prevalent in the 19th century, but with advent of vaccines it is almost eliminated
Maternal Disease States6-8Diabetes, phenylketonuria, endocrinopathies
Drugs and Chemicals1Alcohol, smoking, thalidomide, others (see below)
Other Causes

Examples: cleft lip, cleft palate, neural tube defects
Unknown40-60

Maternal diabetes in pregnancy p. 5

Maternal hyperglycemia→ Fetal hyperinsulinemia→ Fetal macrosomia→ Organomegaly, increased body fat and muscle mass, cardiac anomalies and neural tube defects

Drugs and Chemicals p. 5

AgentEffect
AlcoholCauses fetal alcohol syndrome:
  • Growth restriction
  • Facial anomalies like microcephaly or short palpebral fissures, maxillary hyperplasia
  • Psychomotor disturbances
SmokingHigh incidence of spontaneous abortion and premature labor, placental abnormalities, low birth weight, and SIDS
ThalidomideTranquilizer, teratogenic drug that was prevalent before and led to limb malformations
OthersFolic acid antagonists, androgens, phenytoin, warfarin

Common birth defects (USA, 1999-2001) p. 5

Listed by prevalence per 1,000 live births. Highest listed: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) 12.8 and cleft lip with/without cleft palate 10.5. Also includes trisomy 13 and 18, spina bifida, anencephaly, GIT atresias / TE fistula, gastroschisis, diaphragmatic hernia, omphalocele.

D. Pathogenesis of Congenital Anomalies

Two general principles p. 5

Complex and still poorly understood. Two general principles:

  1. Timing of insult
  2. Interplay between environment and genetic cause

Timing of Prenatal Teratogenic Insult Must Know p. 5

PeriodSusceptibility to teratogens
Embryonic Period (1st-9th week): first 3 weeksInjurious agents (teratogen) may damage enough cells to cause fetal death
Embryonic Period: 3rd to 9th weekExtremely susceptible to teratogens
Peak susceptibility: 4th to 5th week
Fetal PeriodLeast susceptible to teratogens
More susceptible to growth retardation or injury to already formed organs

Interplay Between Environmental Teratogens and Intrinsic Genetic Defects Must Know p. 5-6

TeratogenTypeEffectsUnderlying genetic cause
CyclopaminePlant teratogenEaten by pregnant sheep → lambs with:
  • Craniofacial abnormality
  • Holoprosencephaly (forebrain fails to develop into 2 hemispheres)
  • Cyclopia (single fused eye)
Disruption in the Hedgehog signaling pathway in the embryo
Valproic AcidAntiepileptic drug, known teratogenCauses valproic acid embryopathy:
  • Craniofacial abnormalities: prominent forehead, epicanthal folds, hypoplastic zygomatic arches, shallow philtrum, depressed nasal bridge, posterior angulation of the ears and infraorbital creases
  • Spina bifida
  • Congenital heart defects
  • Developmental delay
Disruption of the expression of homeobox (HOX) proteins
Vitamin A (retinol, retinoic acid for acne)Drug teratogen
Used orally or topically to treat acne
  • CNS defect/s
  • Cardiac defect/s
  • Craniofacial defect/s: cleft lip/palate, microtia (underdeveloped pinna of the ear)
Disruption of TGF-β (transforming growth factor) signaling pathway
Study Aid
Pair each teratogen with its pathway: Cyclopamine → Hedgehog. Valproic acid → HOX. Vitamin A → TGF-β.
Exam Cues (Review Questions)
FALSE about congenital anomalies: "all causes have been explained due to molecular studies." More than half have no explained cause.
Cause of cleft lip and cleft palate → Multifactorial (combination of environmental and genetic).

IV. Prematurity

❗ Must Know
2nd most common cause of neonatal mortality (behind congenital anomalies) in the USA.

Definitions by gestational age p. 6

< 37 wksPremature (gestational age in utero)
37-42 wksMature / term infant
> 42 wksPostmature / post term infant

Issues with postmature / post term infants

  • Carry risks for both mother and infant, including fetal malnutrition
  • After 42 weeks, the placenta starts aging and eventually fails
  • If the fetus passes its fecal matter and breathes it in → meconium aspiration syndrome

Table 9. Important Terms in the Context of Infant Maturity Must Know p. 6

TermDescription
Appropriate for Gestational Age (AGA)Appropriate weight and length of the newborn (i.e., head circumference, body weight, body length)
Large for Gestational Age (LGA)>90th percentile
Small for Gestational Age (SGA)<10th percentile
Low Birth Weight (LBW)<2500 grams
Very Low Birth Weight (VLBW)<1000 grams
  • LBW and VLBW infants are kept in the Neonatal ICU until the infant has matured and can cope without elaborate machine systems.
  • Issues associated with LBW and VLBW infants:
    • Hypothermia
    • Respiratory distress
    • Hyperbilirubinemia
    • Fluid & electrolyte imbalance
    • Susceptibility to infections
    • Feeding problems

Nice to know (APGAR): Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration. Each scored 0, 1, 2 at 1 and 5 minutes after delivery. 7-10 Normal, 4-6 Fairly Low, 0-3 Critically Low.

Risk factorDetails
PPROM
(preterm premature rupture of placental membranes)		Responsible for as many as ⅓ of all preterm deliveries
Risk factors:
  • Prior history of preterm delivery
  • Preterm labor
  • Smoking
  • Mothers in the low socioeconomic status
  • Poor nutrition
Becomes PROM after 37 weeks AOG
Intrauterine Infections Must Know❗ Major cause of preterm labor
  • Chorioamnionitis (inflammation of placental membranes)

  • Most common organisms: Ureaplasma urealyticum, Mycoplasma hominis, Gardnerella vaginalis, Trichomonas, Gonorrhea, Chlamydia

Hazards of prematurity

NRDS (neonatal respiratory distress syndrome) NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis) Sepsis Intraventricular and germinal matrix hemorrhage

B. Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR)

Small for gestational age (SGA) infants p. 7

  • Babies who, even if they are term (not preterm), have LBW.
  • SGA infants:
    • Include term infants but with weight < 2500 g
    • Undergrown rather than immature
    • Suffer from FGR

Causes of FGR Must Know p. 7

CategoryDetailsType of FGR
Fetal abnormalitiesDespite adequate supply of nutrients from the mother, the babies are still not growing properly
May be due to:
  • Chromosomal abnormalities (Trisomies)
  • Congenital anomalies
  • Congenital infections (TORCH): Toxoplasmosis, Other (e.g., syphilis, varicella, mumps, parvovirus, and HIV), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes simplex
❗ Proportionate FGR: symmetric growth restriction
All organs are similarly affected (if the head is small, the chest and body are symmetrically small also)
Placental abnormalitiesUteroplacental insufficiency (uteroplacental blood supply insufficiency)
May be due to:
  • Umbilical-placental vascular anomalies (single umbilical artery, abnormal cord insertion, placenta hemangioma)
  • Placental abruption
  • Placenta previa
  • Placental thrombosis and infarction
  • Placental infections
  • Multiple gestations
❗ Disproportionate FGR: asymmetric growth retardation of fetus
Relative sparing of the brain (the body is a little bit small, the head is not really that affected)
Maternal abnormalities
  • Maternal conditions that decrease placental blood flow
  • Vascular diseases (e.g., preeclampsia / toxemia of pregnancy)
  • Chronic hypertension
  • Thrombophilias (acquired antiphospholipid antibody syndrome)
  • Narcotic abuse, alcohol intake, and heavy cigarette smoking
Not specified in lecture
Key Differentiator
Fetal cause (problem is in the baby) → symmetric: head small too.
Placental cause (supply problem) → asymmetric: brain spared.

Outcome of SGA / FGR p. 7

  • SGA infant faces a difficult course (during perinatal period, childhood, or adult life).
  • Morbidity depends on the cause of FGR and degree of prematurity. May be in the form of:
    • Major handicap
    • Cerebral dysfunction
    • Learning disability
    • Hearing and visual impairment
Exam Trap (Review Q9)
A term infant weighing 2100 g with decreased head circumference and other bodily measurements → proportionate (symmetric) FGR → fetal abnormality such as Toxoplasmosis (TORCH).
Single umbilical artery, placenta previa, chronic villitis → placental abnormalities → disproportionate FGR.

C. Hazards of Prematurity: A. Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome (NRDS)

❗ Must Know
NRDS is the most common cause of RDS in newborn.

Overview p. 7

  • Decrease in cases is due to improvement of management and administration of surfactants.
  • Other causes of RDS in newborn:
    • Excessive sedation of the mother
    • Fetal head injury during delivery
    • Aspiration of blood / amniotic fluid
    • Intrauterine hypoxia due to coiling of umbilical cord around neck
  • Microscopic: deposition of a layer of hyaline proteinaceous material in the peripheral airspaces (alveoli)
    • 📣 Lecturer Dilated alveolar sacs with clear spaces and pinkish lining
    • 📣 Lecturer AKA Hyaline Membrane Disease due to the pinkish membranous material on the alveolar wall

Clinical Course of NRDS p. 7-8

Typical patient: usually preterm or appropriate for gestational age (AGA) infants. Usually male, with mothers with diabetes, those delivered by cesarean section.

At birth: immediate resuscitation. Within a few minutes, rhythmic breathing and normal color are back
↓
After 30 minutes: breathing becomes more difficult
↓
Within a few hours: cyanosis occurs
↓
Full-blown: cyanosis increases. Even 80% oxygen fails to improve the condition of the baby
↓
If therapy prevents death in the first 3-4 days, recovery is excellent

Pathogenesis of NRDS Must Know p. 8

1. Immaturity of the lungs

NRDS is inversely proportional to AOG:

AOGIncidence of NRDS
Less mature infants at 28 weeks60%
28-32 weeks30%
More mature, 34 weeks<5%

Study note: the trans reads "more mature at less than 34 weeks AOG". The row is meant as the more mature group.

2. Deficiency of pulmonary surfactant

  • Surfactant production by Type II alveolar cells is accelerated after 35 weeks AOG.
  • Surfactants reduce surface tension at the air-liquid barrier in the alveoli → less pressure required to keep them patent and aerated.
  • Decreased surfactant → lung collapse with each breath. The infant works as hard with each successive breath.
  • With decreased pulmonary surfactant, progressive atelectasis and reduced lung compliance → hyaline membrane formation in alveolar spaces.
    • Hyaline membranes are barriers to gas exchange → CO2 retention and hypoxemia.
    • Hypoxemia impairs surfactant synthesis → a vicious cycle.

Schematic (Figure 17)

PREMATURITY
↓
Reduced surfactant synthesis, storage, and release
↓
Decreased alveolar surfactant
↓
Increased alveolar surface tension
↓
Atelectasis
↓
Uneven perfusionHypoventilation
↓
Hypoxemia + CO2 retention (↺ feeds back to reduced surfactant synthesis)
↓
Acidosis
↓
Pulmonary vasoconstriction
↓
Pulmonary hypoperfusion
↓
Endothelial damageEpithelial damage
↓
Plasma leak into alveoli
↓
Fibrin + necrotic cells (hyaline membrane) along alveolar walls → restricts proper gas exchange (↺ increased diffusion gradient worsens hypoxemia)

Morphology of NRDS p. 8

Gross: lungs are solid, airless, reddish purple, and sink in water (known as hepatization)

Microscopic:

  • Alveoli are poorly developed, some collapsed
  • (+) eosinophilic hyaline membranes
  • Paucity of neutrophils
Exam Trap
Hyaline membranes are never seen in stillborn infants.

Clinical Features (Prevention) of NRDS p. 8

  • The major thrust in the control of NRDS focuses on prevention:
    • Delaying labor until the fetal lung reaches maturity, or
    • Inducing lung maturation by use of antenatal steroids
  • Critical to this objective: accurate assessment of fetal lung maturity by analysis of amniotic fluid phospholipids
    • Pulmonary secretions are discharged in amniotic fluid → assessing surfactant level.
  • Prophylactic exogenous surfactant at birth to presumed premature infants with gestational age of < 28 weeks has been shown to be very beneficial.
  • With newer ventilation techniques → dramatic improvement in pulmonary function, symptom resolution, and markedly reduced mortality.

Management of NRDS p. 8

  • Giving exogenous surfactant
  • Oxygen administration
  • Complications (even if the infant survives):
    • Retrolental fibroplasia (retinopathy of prematurity)
    • Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
    • These complications are now infrequent due to gentler ventilation techniques, antenatal glucocorticoid therapy, and prophylactic surfactant.
  • Infants who recover from RDS have increased risk for other complications of preterm birth:
    • Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)
    • Intraventricular hemorrhage
    • Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC)
Exam Cues (Review & Formative Quiz)
Risk factors for NRDS: male gender, maternal diabetes mellitus, cesarean delivery, preterm. "Paternal diabetes" is the trap.
Fundamental defect → surfactant deficiency from immature type II pneumocytes.
Hyaline membranes are composed of fibrin and necrotic epithelial cells.

B. Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC)

Epidemiology & Pathogenesis of NEC p. 8-9

  • Most common in premature infants
  • Incidence is inversely proportional to AOG

Pathogenesis

  • Uncertain, most likely multifactorial
  • Most cases are associated with enteral feeding
  • Suggests postnatal insult (e.g., introduction of bacteria) sets in motion the cascade culminating in tissue destruction
  • No single bacteria has been linked
  • Role of PAF (platelet activating factor), which increases mucosal permeability, is being studied as the cause of NEC

Morphology of NEC Must Know p. 9

Gross:

  • Usually involves terminal ileum, cecum, and right colon
  • Involved segment is distended, friable and congested with hemorrhagic infarction or is gangrenous
  • Submucosal gas bubbles (pneumatosis intestinalis)

Microscopic: mucosal or transmural coagulative necrosis, ulceration, bacterial colonization, submucosal gas bubbles

Exam Cues (Formative Quiz)
3-day-old premature infant, 1200 g, bloody stools, abdominal distention, gas within the intestinal walls → NEC.
Associated with prematurity, low birth weight, and early enteral (especially formula) feeding. Cesarean delivery is NOT a recognized predisposing factor.
Microscopy of involved bowel → transmural necrosis.

V. Perinatal Infections

2 Routes of perinatal infection Must Know p. 9

Transcervical (ascending)Transplacental (hematologic)
OrganismsMost are bacterial, a few are viral (HSV-2)Mostly parasitic (toxoplasma, malaria) and viral, few are bacterial (Listeria, Treponema)
How fetus is infectedBy inhaling infected amniotic fluid or by passing thru an infected birth canalMicrobes gain access to the fetal bloodstream transplacentally via the chorionic villi
Timing / consequenceConsequence: preterm birthMay occur anytime during gestation, or at the time of delivery via maternal-to-fetal transmission (Hep B, HIV, TORCH group of infections)

A. Parvovirus B19 p. 9

May result in:

  • Spontaneous abortion in the 2nd trimester
  • Stillbirth
  • Hydrops fetalis
  • Congenital anemia

B. Perinatal Sepsis Must Know p. 9

Early onsetLate onset
TimingWithin first 7 days of lifeFrom 7 days to 3 months
PresentationMay cause pneumonia, sepsis, meningitis
Most common causeGroup B StreptococcusListeria and Candida

VI. Fetal Hydrops

Definition p. 9

  • Accumulation of edema fluid in the fetus during intrauterine growth
  • Progressive, generalized edema → lethal
  • May be localized, like pleural and peritoneal effusions, or postnatal (cystic hygroma) → all compatible with life
  • Two types: Immune hydrops and Non-immune hydrops

Table 10. Causes of Hydrops Fetalis p. 9

CategoryCauses
CardiovascularMalformations, tachyarrhythmia, high-output failure
ChromosomalTurner syndrome, trisomy 21, trisomy 18
Thoracic CausesCystic adenomatoid malformation, diaphragmatic hernia
Fetal AnemiaHomozygous alpha-thalassemia, Parvovirus B19, immune hydrops (Rh, ABO)
Twin GestationTwin-to-twin transfusion
InfectionCMV, syphilis, toxoplasmosis
OthersGenitourinary tract malformations
Tumors
Genetic / metabolic disorders

A. Immune Hydrops Must Know p. 9-10

  • Hemolytic disease caused by blood group antigen incompatibility between mother and fetus
  • Rh and ABO blood groups
  • When fetus inherits red cell antigens from the father that are foreign to the mother, a maternal immune reaction may occur
RhABO
Reaction occurs in the 2nd and subsequent pregnancies
Mother Rh-, father Rh+		 Firstborn may be affected
e.g., infant's blood type A or B, mother's type O

Pathogenesis of Immune Hydrops (Figure 23)

Fetal red cells reach the maternal circulation during the last trimester (cytotrophoblast no longer a barrier) or during childbirth
↓
Mother becomes sensitized to the foreign antigen
↓
Initial exposure to Rh Ag → IgM antibodies, which do not cross the placenta → Rh disease is uncommon with the 1st pregnancy
↓
Subsequent pregnancy → brisk IgG response → crosses placenta → antibody attachment to Rh+ erythrocytes
↓
Removal and destruction of erythrocyte-antibody complex
↓
Branch 1: Anemia
↓
Extramedullary hematopoiesis
Cardiac decompensation
↓
Hydrops
Branch 2: Hemoglobin degradation
↓
Bilirubin
↓
Jaundice, Kernicterus

Consequences of Excessive RBC Destruction in Immune Hydrops Must Know p. 10

Anemia

  • Direct result of red cell loss
If severe → hypoxic injury to heart & liver→ ↓ plasma proteins (liver injury) & cardiac failure→ ↓ plasma oncotic pressure & ↑ hydrostatic pressure→ Generalized edema

Jaundice

Hemolysis → unconjugated bilirubin→ Passes through poorly developed blood brain barrier→ Binds to lipids in the brain→ CNS damage (kernicterus)
Exam Cues (Formative Quiz)
Substance that accumulates in the brain → bilirubin (kernicterus: unconjugated bilirubin deposits in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei).
Enlarged liver in hemolytic disease of the newborn → extramedullary hematopoiesis with islands of red cell precursors.

B. Non-Immune Hydrops p. 10

3 major causes:

CVS defectsChromosomal abnormalitiesFetal anemia
  • Turner syndrome, Trisomies 21 & 18 are associated with fetal hydrops due to accompanying structural cardiac anomalies.
    • In Turner syndrome: cystic hygromas may result from abnormalities in lymphatic drainage from the neck.
  • Fetal Anemia (not caused by Rh- or ABO-associated antibodies) may result from:
    • Homozygous α-thalassemia (most common in Southeast Asia)
    • Parvovirus B19 infection

VII. Inborn Errors of Metabolism (IEM)

Overview p. 10

  • Well-characterized genetic disorders that give rise to metabolic disorders
  • Most are rare diseases, autosomal recessive or X-linked
  • 3 disorders discussed: Phenylketonuria (PKU), Galactosemia, Cystic Fibrosis
  • Newborn Screening Tests: for the detection of inborn errors of metabolism
    • 📣 Lecturer There is a law in the Philippines that all newborns should undergo screening tests.

Newborn screening: panel of 22 disorders (Figure 26) p. 10

MethodNo.Disorders
DELFIA system4Congenital hypothyroidism
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Galactosemia
Biotinidase deficiency
Tandem MS/MS18Aminoacidopathies: ASA, CIT, PKU, MSUD, HCYS, TYR-1
Organic acidemias: MMA, PPA, MCD, MCC, IVA, PKT, GA1, HMG
Fatty acid oxidation defects: MCAD, VLCAD, LCHAD, TFPD

A. Table 11. Abnormalities Suggesting Inborn Errors of Metabolism p. 10

SystemAbnormalities
GeneralDysmorphic features, deafness, self-mutilation, abnormal hair, abnormal body and urine odor, hepatosplenomegaly, cardiomegaly, hydrops
NeurologicHypotonia, hypertonia, coma, persistent lethargy, seizures

B. Phenylketonuria (PKU)

Phenylketonuria Must Know p. 10-11

Inheritance: Autosomal recessive

Cause: Severe deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH)

↓ PAH→ Inability to convert phenylalanine → tyrosine→ Rising phenylalanine impairs brain development

Management: dietary restriction of phenylalanine

  • Phenylalanine is found in most foods rich in protein: beef, fish, eggs, milk, yogurt, cheese, soybean, tofu, certain nuts and seeds.
  • Artificial sweeteners such as aspartame are also high in phenylalanine.
    • In babies with PKU, avoid giving these foods.

Clinical picture of PKU

  • Babies are normal at birth. Within a few weeks, rising phenylalanine impairs brain development.
  • Within 6 months → severe mental retardation
    • ⅓ never able to walk, ⅔ cannot talk
  • Seizures
  • Eczema, decreased pigmentation of hair and skin (decreased tyrosine, a precursor for melanin)
  • Strong musty or mousy odor in the sweat and urine

C. Galactosemia

Galactosemia Must Know p. 11

Inheritance: Autosomal recessive disorder of galactose metabolism

Cause: Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in tissues (liver, spleen, lens of the eye, kidneys, heart muscle, cerebral cortex, erythrocytes)

VariantTotal lack of GALTDeficiency of galactokinase
EnzymeGALT: galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferaseGalactokinase
FrequencyMore commonRare variant
SeverityMild
Not associated with mental retardation

Clinical course of Galactosemia

TimingFinding
Almost from birthFailure to thrive
Within a few days of milk ingestionVomiting and diarrhea
1st few weeksJaundice and hepatomegaly, cataracts
6 to 12 monthsMental retardation (not as severe as PKU)

Management: early removal of galactose from diet

D. Cystic Fibrosis (Mucoviscidosis)

Overview Must Know p. 11

  • Inherited disorder of ion transport
  • Affects fluid secretion in exocrine glands and in the epithelial lining of the respiratory, GIT, and reproductive tracts
  • More common in caucasians
Abnormally viscous secretions that obstruct organ passages→ Chronic lung disease 2° to recurrent infections
Pancreatic insufficiency, steatorrhea, malnutrition
Hepatic cirrhosis
Intestinal obstruction
Male infertility

CFTR chloride channel defect (Figure 29) p. 11

Sweat glandAirway
Chloride channel defect → increased Cl⁻ & Na⁺ in sweat ↓ Cl⁻ secretion & ↑ Na⁺ & H₂O reabsorption
→ dehydration of the mucus layer coating epithelial cells
→ defective mucociliary action
→ mucus plugging of airways
  • The most common mutation of the CFTR gene results in defective protein folding (Golgi / endoplasmic reticulum) and degradation of the CFTR before it reaches the cell surface.
  • More than 1800 mutations of the CFTR gene.

Clinical spectrum vs sweat test (Figure 30) p. 11

  • If the sweat test is positive, you can have the symptoms. If negative, you can have normal or mild symptoms.
Classical Cystic Fibrosis: bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, male infertility, hepatic cirrhosis (sweat test positive, severe CFTR abnormality)
↓
Meconium ileus, pancreatic insufficiency, mild lung disease
↓
Bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, male infertility
↓
Mild lung disease, polyposis, pancreatic insufficiency
↓
Sinusitis, absent vas deferens
↓
Azoospermia
↓
(Normal female) (sweat test negative, mild CFTR abnormality)

Table 12. Clinical Features of Cystic Fibrosis p. 12

FeatureDetails
Chronic Sinopulmonary DiseasePersistent infection with CF pathogens
Chronic cough & sputum production
Nasal polyps
Gastrointestinal and Nutritional AbnormalitiesIntestinal: meconium ileus, rectal prolapse
Pancreatic: recurrent acute pancreatitis
Hepatic: cirrhosis, prolonged neonatal jaundice
Nutritional
Salt-loss syndromeAcute salt depletion
Chronic metabolic alkalosis
Male Urogenital AbnormalitiesResulting to obstructive azoospermia

Criteria for Diagnosis of Cystic Fibrosis Must Know p. 12

MUST HAVE (any one)COUPLED WITH (any one)
  • One or more characteristic features
  • OR a history of CF in a sibling
  • OR a positive newborn screening test
  • An increased sweat chloride concentration on 2 or more occasions
  • OR identification of 2 CF mutations
  • OR demonstration of abnormal epithelial nasal ion transport

Morphology of Cystic Fibrosis p. 12

Table 13. Mutations (Classes) of the CFTR gene p. 12

ClassDefect
Class IDefective protein synthesis (complete lack of CFTR protein)
Class IIAbnormal protein folding, processing, and trafficking
Class IIIDefective regulation
Class IVDecreased conductance
Class VReduced abundance
Class VIAltered function in the regulation of ion channels

VIII. Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS)

Definition Must Know p. 12

  • AKA Crib death
  • Sudden death of an infant under 1 year of age
  • Death remains unexplained after a thorough case investigation, including:
    • Autopsy
    • Exam of death scene
    • Review of clinical history
  • Diagnosis of exclusion
    • 📣 Lecturer You must rule out first other causes of death.

A. Clinical Features of SIDS p. 12

  • Infant usually dies at home while asleep, mostly in a prone or side position, usually at night
  • 90% occur in the 1st 6 months (between 2-4 months)
  • Supine sleeping position: the only safe position that reduces risk of SIDS (American Academy of Pediatrics)
< 1 yrAge in definition
90%In 1st 6 months
2-4 moPeak
SupineOnly safe sleep position

Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) Must Know p. 12-13

  • Many cases of SIDS may have an unexpected anatomic or biochemical basis discernible at autopsy.
  • When thorough investigation discovers an underlying cause (e.g., infections causing viral myocarditis or bronchopneumonia, congenital anomaly, congenital aortic stenosis), it is no longer SIDS but rather called SUID.

Table 15. Postmortem Abnormalities Detected in Cases of SUID

CategoryExamples
InfectionsViral myocarditis, bronchopneumonia
Unsuspected congenital anomalyCongenital aortic stenosis, ALCAPA (anomalous origin of the left coronary artery)
Traumatic child abuse
Intentional suffocation (Filicide)Murder of one's own daughter / son
Genetic and metabolic defectsLong QT syndrome, fatty acid oxidation disorders, histiocytoid cardiomyopathy, abnormal inflammatory responsiveness

B. Pathogenesis of SIDS Must Know p. 12

Multifactorial, triple risk model:

(1) Vulnerable infant
(parents or infants)
(2) Critical developmental period
in homeostatic period during the 1st 6 months of life
(3) Exogenous stressor
(e.g., environment)
  • Most compelling hypothesis: SIDS reflects delayed development of arousal and cardiorespiratory control.
    • The brainstem (i.e., medulla) plays a critical role in the body's arousal response to noxious stimuli during sleep:
      • Episodic hypercarbia
      • Hypoxia
      • Thermal stress

C. Table 14. Risk Factors Associated with SIDS p. 12-13

GroupRisk factors
PARENTAL
  • Young maternal age such as < 20 y/o
  • Maternal smoking during pregnancy
  • Drug abuse in either parent, such as paternal marijuana, maternal opiate, and cocaine use
  • Short intergestational intervals
  • Late or no prenatal care
  • Low socioeconomic status
  • African American and American Indian ethnicity
INFANT
  • Brain stem abnormalities, associated with delayed development of arousal and cardiorespiratory control
  • Prematurity and low birth weight
  • Male sex
  • Product of multiple birth
  • SIDS in a prior sibling
  • Antecedent respiratory infections
  • Germline polymorphisms in autonomic nervous system genes
ENVIRONMENT
  • Prone or side sleep position, sleeping on soft surface
  • Hyperthermia
  • Co-sleeping (sleeping with parents) in the 1st 3 months of life
Do Not Confuse
SIDS = death remains unexplained after full investigation.
SUID = an underlying cause is found at autopsy or investigation.

IX. Tumors and Tumor-Like Lesions

Malignant vs benign tumors in childhood p. 13

Malignant neoplasms (rank as cause of death)Benign tumors
1-4 y/o: 4th most common cause of death
4-9 y/o: 2nd most common cause of death
9-14 y/o: 2nd most common cause of death		 More common than malignant
Of little concern, but occasionally cause serious complications due to location or rapid increase in size

A. Tumor-Like Lesions

Heterotopia (Choristoma) vs Hamartoma Must Know p. 13

Heterotopia (Choristoma)Hamartoma
DefinitionNormal cells or tissues present in ABNORMAL locationsExcessive focal overgrowth of cells and tissues native to the organ in which it occurs
CellsNormal cellsCells are mature and identical to the native cells, but they do not reproduce the normal architecture of the surrounding tissue
SignificanceOf little significance, but can be confused clinically with neoplasms
Rarely sites of origin of true neoplasms, like adrenal carcinoma in ovary
ExamplesRest of pancreatic tissue in stomach or small intestine
Mass of adrenal cells in kidney, lungs, ovaries		Some consider these as hamartomas: hemangioma, lymphangioma, rhabdomyoma, liver adenoma, developmental cysts in kidneys / lungs / pancreas
Do Not Confuse
Heterotopia = normal tissue in the wrong place.
Hamartoma = native tissue in the right place, overgrown and disorganized.

B. Benign Tumors

Hemangioma Must Know p. 13

  • Most common tumors of infancy
  • May be of cavernous or capillary types
  • Seen mostly on skin (esp. on face and scalp)
  • Flat to elevated, red blue
    • If flat: "port-wine stains"
  • May enlarge as the child grows
  • Usually spontaneously regress

Lymphangioma vs Lymphangiectasis p. 13

LymphangiomaLymphangiectasis
  • May increase in size after birth due to fluid accumulation
    • May encroach on vital structures
  • Does not extend beyond its original location
  • Usually involves: skin, deep regions of neck, axilla, mediastinum, retroperitoneal
  • Abnormal dilatations of pre-existing lymph channels
  • Presents as a diffuse swelling of part or all of an extremity

Fibrous Tumors p. 13

  • Fibromatosis
  • Infantile Fibrosarcoma
    • Excellent prognosis
    • Chromosomal translocation t(12;15)(p13;q25)

Teratomas Must Know p. 13-14

  • 2 peaks:
    • At 2 years old
    • Late adolescence and early adulthood
  • Mature, immature, malignant teratomas

Sacrococcygeal Teratomas

❗ Must Know
Sacrococcygeal teratoma: most common teratoma in childhood
  • Girls > boys
  • 75% are benign (esp. if <4 y/o)
  • 12% malignant and lethal (esp. if older children)
  • Location: hindgut, testis, ovaries, mediastinum, retroperitoneum, head and neck

C. Malignant Tumors

How childhood malignant tumors differ from adult counterparts Must Know p. 14

Differ biologically and histologically, based on their:

  • Incidence and type of tumor
  • Close relationship between abnormal development (teratogenesis) and tumor induction (oncogenesis)
  • ❗ Tendency to regress or differentiate spontaneously
  • Improved survival or cure of many childhood tumors

Incidence: sharp peaks (<10 y/o) p. 14

❗ Must Know
1. Leukemia (ALL): most deaths in <15 y/o than all others combined
  1. Neuroblastoma
  2. Wilms tumor
  3. Hepatoblastoma
  4. Retinoblastoma
  5. Rhabdomyosarcoma
  6. Teratoma
  7. Ewing sarcoma
  8. Juvenile astrocytoma
  9. Medulloblastoma
  10. Ependymoma

ChildrenAdult
  • Hematopoietic (leukemia)
  • Nervous (including adrenal and retina)
  • Soft tissue

Histologic features of childhood tumors p. 14

  • More primitive looking, undifferentiated
  • May show features of organogenesis specific to site of tumor (suffix -blastoma)
  • Sheets of cells with small, round nuclei → collectively called Small Round Blue Cell tumors
Exam Trap (Review Q10)
FALSE about childhood malignant tumors: "mostly involve the skin, lung, breast, prostate, and colon" (those are adult types).
No. 1 malignancy in infants is leukemia, which is hematopoietic.

Neuroblastoma

General features Must Know p. 14

  • Derived from primordial neural crest cells in adrenal medulla and sympathetic ganglia
  • Spontaneous or therapy-induced differentiation into mature elements
  • Spontaneous tumor regression
    • May cause fibrosis / calcification
    • Does not happen in adults (only seen in children)
  • Most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood
  • Most frequently diagnosed tumor of infancy
  • Median age at diagnosis: 1½ years (18 months)
  • Location:
    • 40% adrenal medulla
    • 25% paravertebral of abdomen
    • 15% posterior mediastinum
    • Others: pelvis, neck, brain
  • Most are sporadic (1-2% are familial)
  • Germline mutations in the anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) gene: observed in familial and 10% of sporadic

Microscopic findings p. 14

  • Small, primitive-appearing cells with dark nuclei, scanty cytoplasm, poorly defined cell borders, growing in solid sheets
  • Neuropil (fibrillary material)
  • Rosettes (rosette formation)
    • 📣 Lecturer Flowerlike formation with central core (space) surrounded by layers of dark staining cells

Clinical course Must Know p. 14

<2 y/o patientsOlder children
Present with large abdominal mass, fever, weight loss Clinically recognized when metastatic symptoms are present: bone pain, respiratory and GIT complaints
  • Metastasize widely through hematogenous and lymphatic routes → into liver, lungs, bones, or bone marrow
  • 90% produce catecholamines (diagnostic)
    • Increased blood levels
    • Increased urine levels of the metabolites:
      • VMA (Vanillylmandelic acid)
      • HVA (Homovanillic acid)
  • Disseminated neuroblastomas in neonates
    • Present with multiple cutaneous metastases (deep blue discoloration)
❗ Must Know
Disseminated neuroblastoma in neonates → "blueberry muffin baby"

Histology: evidence of schwannian stroma and gangliocytic differentiation ❗PresentAbsent
Mitosis-karyorrhexis index<200/5000 cells>200/5000 cells
DNA ploidyHyperdiploid (whole chromosomal gains)Near-diploid (segmental chromosomal losses, chromothripsis)
MYCN ❗Not AmplifiedAmplified

Age: <18 months → more favorable
Evidence of schwannian stroma: present → more favorable
Amplification of the MYCN oncogene: unfavorable prognosis. 20-30% of tumors present as advanced-stage disease. Most important genetic abnormality used in risk stratification.

Wilms Tumor

General features Must Know p. 15

❗ Must Know
Most common primary renal tumor in children
  • 4th most common pediatric malignancy
  • Peak age: 2-5 years old
    • 95% occur before 10 years old
    • 📣 Lecturer In cases, this is usually 5 years old with hematuria
  • 5-10% bilateral (synchronous or metachronous)

Pathogenesis of Wilms Tumor Must Know p. 15

Increased risk with 3 groups of congenital malformations with chromosomal loci:

SyndromeFeaturesGenetics
WAGR SyndromeWilms tumor, Aniridia, Genital anomalies, mental RetardationDeletions of 11p13, WT1 gene
Two-hit theory of recessive tumor suppressor genes
Denys-Drash SyndromeGonadal dysgenesis, nephropathyAlso with germline abnormality in WT1
Beckwith-Wiedemann SyndromeOrganomegaly, macroglossia, hemihypertrophy, omphalocele, adrenal cytomegalyBand 11p15.5 ("WT2," distal to WT1 locus)

Microscopic findings Must Know p. 15

Attempts to recapitulate different stages of nephrogenesis:

ComponentAppearance
BlastemalTightly packed blue cells
📣 Lecturer Aggregates of small dark cells
EpithelialPrimitive tubules
📣 Lecturer See tubule, gland-like
StromalFibrocystic or myxoid
📣 Lecturer Pinkish, elongated, fibrous or myxoid stromal component

Clinical features p. 15

  • Large abdominal masses
  • Hematuria, abdominal pain
  • Present cure rate: 90%
  • 3 adverse prognosis:
    • Anaplasia
    • Loss of genetic material on chromosome 11q and 16q
    • Gain of chromosome 1q
  • Increased risk of developing 2nd primary tumors: due to germline mutation or therapy-induced (radiation)

Neuroblastoma vs Wilms Tumor

NeuroblastomaWilms Tumor
Claim to fameMost common extracranial solid tumor of childhood
Most frequently diagnosed tumor of infancy		Most common primary renal tumor in children
4th most common pediatric malignancy

MicroscopySmall round cells, neuropil, rosettesBlastemal, epithelial, stromal components
Clinical clueAbdominal mass, catecholamines (VMA, HVA), blueberry muffin babyLarge abdominal mass, hematuria, abdominal pain
PrognosisFavorable: <18 mo, schwannian stroma, MYCN not amplifiedCure rate 90%. Adverse: anaplasia, 11q/16q loss, 1q gain

InheritanceAutosomal recessiveAutosomal recessiveInherited. More common in caucasians
OnsetNormal at birth. Brain impaired within weeks. Severe MR within 6 monthsFailure to thrive almost from birth. Vomiting / diarrhea after milk. MR in 6-12 monthsMeconium ileus to mild disease (spectrum)

Severity of MRSevere (⅓ never walk, ⅔ cannot talk)Not as severe as PKU. Galactokinase variant: no MR
ManagementDietary restriction of phenylalanine (avoid protein foods, aspartame)Early removal of galactose from diet

Cram Sheet

❗ Red-exclamation points (lecture wording)

  1. Congenital anomalies: most common cause of mortality in the 1st year (USA)
  2. Prematurity: 2nd most common cause of neonatal mortality (behind congenital anomalies) in the USA
  3. Intrauterine infections: major cause of preterm labor
  4. Fetal abnormalities → usually leads to proportionate FGR: symmetric growth restriction
    • All organs similarly affected
  5. Placental abnormalities → usually leads to disproportionate FGR: asymmetric growth retardation of fetus
    • Relative sparing of the brain
  6. NRDS: most common cause of RDS in newborn
  7. Sacrococcygeal teratomas: most common teratoma in childhood
  8. Childhood malignant tumors: tendency to regress or differentiate spontaneously
  9. Leukemia (ALL): #1 sharp peak. Most deaths in <15 y/o than all others combined
  10. Disseminated neuroblastoma in neonates: "blueberry muffin baby" (multiple cutaneous metastases, deep blue)
  11. Neuroblastoma prognostic variables noted by doc:
    • Age <18 months → more favorable
    • Schwannian stroma present → more favorable
    • MYCN amplification → unfavorable. Most important genetic abnormality used in risk stratification
  12. Wilms tumor: most common primary renal tumor in children

Causes of death (know the top 2)

AgeUSA #1, #2PH #1, #2
<1 yrCongenital anomalies, Prematurity/LBWBacterial sepsis, Pneumonia
1-4Accidents, Congenital anomaliesPneumonia, Diarrhea/GE
5-9Accidents, MalignancyPneumonia, Dengue/DHF
10-14Accidents, MalignancyPneumonia, Accidental drowning
  • PH: top causes mostly infectious (developing country). Congenital anomalies 3rd in 1-4 in PH.
  • USA <1 yr: bacterial sepsis of newborn = only infectious cause on the list.

Core definitions

  • Congenital anomalies: anatomic defects present at birth. "Born with". Does not imply or exclude genetic basis (e.g., congenital syphilis)
  • Malformation: intrinsically abnormal developmental process
  • Deformation: extrinsic disturbance. Compression of fetus. Most common factor: uterine constraint (35th-38th weeks)
  • Disruption: secondary destruction of a previously normal organ. Extrinsic. NOT hereditary (amniotic band)
  • Sequence: cascade of anomalies triggered by one initiating aberration (Potter)
  • Malformation syndrome: multiple anomalies that cannot be explained by a single localized initiating defect. Single etiologic agent
  • Agenesis = complete absence of organ or primordium. Aplasia = failure of growth of existing primordium. Atresia = absence of an opening
  • Hypoplasia/Hyperplasia = number. Hypotrophy/Hypertrophy = size. Dysplasia = abnormal organization, precursor of carcinoma
  • Fetal hydrops: accumulation of edema fluid in the fetus. Progressive generalized edema is lethal. Localized / cystic hygroma compatible with life
  • SIDS: sudden death of infant <1 year, unexplained after autopsy, death scene exam, clinical history. Diagnosis of exclusion
  • Heterotopia (choristoma): normal tissue in abnormal location. Hamartoma: overgrowth of tissue native to the organ

Mechanisms (short flows)

Potter sequence:

Renal agenesis / amniotic leak / uteroplacental insufficiency→Oligohydramnios→Fetal compression (+ amnion nodosum)→Pulmonary hypoplasia, altered (flattened) facies, clubbed feet, breech

NRDS:

Prematurity → ↓ surfactant→↑ surface tension → atelectasis→Hypoxemia + CO₂ retention (↺ impairs surfactant)→Acidosis → vasoconstriction → hypoperfusion→Endothelial / epithelial damage → plasma leak→Hyaline membrane (fibrin + necrotic cells)

Immune hydrops (Rh):

Fetal RBCs enter mother (last trimester / childbirth)→1st: IgM (no placental crossing)→Later pregnancy: IgG crosses→Hemolysis→Anemia → hydrops
Bilirubin → kernicterus

Anemia → edema:

Severe anemia → hypoxic injury to heart & liver→↓ plasma proteins + cardiac failure→↓ oncotic, ↑ hydrostatic pressure→Generalized edema

Maternal diabetes:

Maternal hyperglycemia→Fetal hyperinsulinemia→Macrosomia: organomegaly, ↑ fat and muscle, cardiac anomalies, NTDs

PKU:

↓ PAH→Phenylalanine not converted to tyrosine→Brain damage (MR) + ↓ melanin (↓ pigment)

Cystic fibrosis (airway):

↓ Cl⁻ secretion, ↑ Na⁺/H₂O reabsorption→Dehydrated mucus→Defective mucociliary action→Mucus plugging

Common confusions & exam traps

  • Hyaline membranes are never seen in stillborn infants.
  • NRDS risk is maternal diabetes, not paternal.
  • NEC: cesarean delivery is NOT a recognized predisposing factor.
  • Rh disease is uncommon in the 1st pregnancy (IgM does not cross placenta). ABO can affect the firstborn.
  • Disruption is NOT hereditary → no risk for subsequent pregnancies.
  • Galactokinase deficiency: rare, mild, no MR. GALT lack: more common.
  • Galactosemia MR is not as severe as PKU.
  • Postmature infants (>42 wks): placenta ages and fails, meconium aspiration syndrome.
  • Spontaneous tumor regression in neuroblastoma does not happen in adults.
  • NRDS complications: retinopathy of prematurity, bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Survivors also at risk of PDA, IVH, NEC.
  • Supine = only safe sleep position. Prone or side, soft surface, hyperthermia, co-sleeping in 1st 3 months = risk.
  • SIDS most compelling hypothesis: delayed development of arousal and cardiorespiratory control (brainstem / medulla).
  • Wilms adverse prognosis: anaplasia, loss of 11q and 16q, gain of 1q. Risk of 2nd primary tumors.
